strengths: Addresses a practically important problem — reducing visual token count for VLM video understanding under latency/memory constraints — and reports substantial efficiency gains (72% GPU memory reduction, ~24% latency reduction).

The retrieve-then-compress pipeline (event-based segmentation + query-relevant retrieval, followed by temporal token merging and RL-based distillation) is a reasonable and intuitively motivated design that combines ideas from Video-RAG and token-merging literature.

Extensive empirical evaluation across six diverse benchmarks (both video reasoning and general video QA) with several baselines and models (Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL3.5, Gemma-3, ByteVideoLLM, MovieChat, VidCom2).
Reasonably thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of VMR alone, C-GRPO alone, comparison against SFT/SFT+VMR, and sensitivity to the retention threshold τ.
The reported result of near-baseline mean accuracy (42.20 vs 42.21) with ~95% token reduction is an appealing headline number if the underlying evaluation is sound.
weaknesses: The core novelty of C-GRPO is limited: it is essentially GRPO with an added scalar retention-ratio bonus gated by a correctness indicator (Eq. 7-8); the technical contribution beyond reward engineering is thin relative to the claim of being a fundamentally new RL strategy.

Fairness of baseline comparisons is questionable: MARC benefits from the VMR retrieval stage (which alone raises mean score from 42.21 to 45.56, Table 2) while competing compression baselines (ByteVideoLLM, MovieChat, VidCom2) are not given the same retrieval-augmented input; this conflates the gains from retrieval versus the RL compression algorithm and makes the reported large margins (65%, 31%, 52%) potentially misleading.

The paper glosses over the degraded performance on long-video benchmarks (VideoMME retains only 74% of baseline performance with 3.21% of tokens), which is arguably the most stringent test of the method (long, information-dense video, single-frame-equivalent budget). This weakens the central claim of "nearly identical" performance under extreme compression.

τ ablation differences (41.34 vs 42.20 vs 41.40, Table 3) are small and no variance/multiple-seed results are reported anywhere, making it hard to assess statistical significance of the reported gains.

Potential data leakage/overlap is not addressed: the training data (Video-R1-260K) is drawn from public video datasets that may overlap in source videos or distributions with the evaluation benchmarks (e.g., MVBench, VideoMME components), which is not discussed or controlled for.

Insufficient detail/clarity on the teacher-student training loop: it is unclear whether the teacher network is frozen, how afull (teacher reward) is computed at each training step (added compute cost), and how compute-heavy the 64-frame teacher rollout is during RL training — reproducibility is weak given these gaps plus reliance on an unincluded appendix (with a broken "Appendix ??" reference).
Only a single model scale (3B) and one backbone (Qwen2.5-VL) is used for the main method; no results on larger models or alternative backbones to demonstrate generality of the approach.

The elaborate cognitive-science motivation (episodic memory, event segmentation theory, neuroimaging) is not tightly connected to concrete algorithmic choices beyond standard shot-boundary detection and embedding-based retrieval, giving an impression of overclaiming conceptual novelty relative to the actual technical mechanism.
No qualitative analysis, failure case discussion, or error analysis is provided to help understand when/why the compression succeeds or fails, particularly on the weaker VideoMME results.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem—reducing token counts for video-LLMs—with a comprehensive efficiency evaluation (72% GPU memory reduction, 23.9% latency reduction) that is grounded in real measurements on a single GPU.
Evaluation spans six diverse benchmarks covering both reasoning and general video understanding, giving a reasonably broad picture of performance retention under compression.

Reasonably thorough ablation studies: effect of the retention threshold τ, isolated contribution of VMR vs. C-GRPO, and comparison against an SFT-based distillation baseline, which helps disentangle the two proposed components.

The retrieve-then-compress pipeline is intuitively motivated and the reported near-parity mean score (42.20 vs 42.21) against a 64-frame baseline while using ~5% of the tokens is an appealing headline result if it generalizes.
Reasonable coverage of related training-free and RAG-style compression baselines in Section 2, situating the contribution within the literature.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is limited: VMR is essentially standard shot-segmentation + embedding retrieval (existing off-the-shelf components: TransNet v2 and a pretrained embedding model), and C-GRPO is GRPO plus a simple correctness-gated retention-ratio bonus—an incremental reward-shaping addition rather than a fundamentally new RL algorithm.

The formulation of the compression reward is underspecified: it is unclear how a_full and a_comp (average rewards under 64-frame vs. compressed input) are computed per training step/batch, whether the teacher is run online for every sample, and how this interacts with GRPO's group-relative advantage estimation—this hampers reproducibility.

Headline 'near-identical mean performance' obscures large disparities across benchmarks: MARC retains only 74% of baseline performance on VideoMME (long videos) while exceeding baseline on some short-video benchmarks; averaging masks this failure mode and the paper's framing somewhat overstates general applicability.

Comparisons to prior compression methods are inconsistent/confusing: the text says the method is compared to 'DynamicVLM' but Table 1 and its caption list 'ByteVideoLLM' instead, suggesting possible errors in reporting or result attribution.

Missing comparisons to well-known, more competitive recent training-free/training-based token compression baselines (e.g., FastV, VisionZip, PruMerge, SparseVLM, which are even cited in the related work) — only three relatively weaker baselines are actually benchmarked.

VMR relies on pre-indexing/embedding an entire video corpus before retrieval, which appears to conflict with the paper's stated real-time/streaming applications (autonomous driving, surveillance) where the whole video is not available in advance.

No variance/seed information, statistical significance testing, or robustness analysis (e.g., different top-k, different backbones) is reported, and the method is validated only on a single backbone (Qwen2.5-VL-3B), limiting evidence of generality.

The cognitive-science motivation for VMR (episodic memory, event segmentation theory) is largely decorative narrative rather than a substantive mechanistic connection reflected in the actual algorithm, which is a standard retrieval + merge pipeline.

Minor writing/consistency issues (e.g., duplicate 'SuperCLEVR' in appendix lists, inconsistent baseline naming) suggest the manuscript would benefit from a more careful proofreading and result-table cross-check pass.
